stem.text: There are different measures of the money supply from narrow money to broad money.

options.text: because different countries have their own national measures of money supply
because of disagreement among economists over the importance of money supply
because of the need to produce different measures of inflation
because of the need to reflect the different functions that money performs

explanation.text: Money performs several distinct functions — medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account, standard of deferred payment — and different assets satisfy these functions to different degrees. Narrow money measures only the most liquid assets usable as a medium of exchange (cash, sight deposits), while broad money includes less liquid assets that still function as a store of value (savings deposits, near-money). Having a range of measures lets economists capture money's different roles.

optionAnalysis.text: While countries may define their measures slightly differently in practice, this is not the underlying reason the narrow/broad distinction exists conceptually.
Disagreement among economists (e.g. monetarists vs Keynesians) is about the importance of controlling the money supply, not the reason multiple measures of its size exist.
Measures of inflation (like different price indices) are a separate statistical issue from measures of the money supply; the two are not defined for the same purpose.
Different assets perform money's functions to different degrees, so narrow and broad measures exist to capture these different degrees of 'moneyness' (liquidity and function).

reasoningChain: Recall the functions of money: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account, standard of deferred payment.

Recognise that not all financial assets perform all these functions equally well — cash is a perfect medium of exchange but earns no interest, while savings accounts are a better store of value but less immediately spendable.
Conclude that narrow and broad money measures exist to capture this spectrum of how well different assets fulfil money's various functions.

inferredMistakes.text: Assuming the different measures exist purely for international comparability or statistical convenience, rather than recognising the underlying economic reason: different assets serve money's functions to different degrees.
